item.title: Kimi, MiniMax Code, and ZCode in OpenResearch: A Fork in One Evening with Claude Opus 5.5
item.description:
OpenResearch from alphaXiv turns coding agents into research agents. It initially supported Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor, and Google Antigravity. I wanted to integrate three more agents I had on Windows: Kimi Code, MiniMax Code, and ZCode. I tasked Claude Code with this in a cloud session, and it produced a fork with releases for Windows and Linux, where the new agents work alongside the old ones. I'll explain what OpenResearch is, how we divided the work, how adapters are structured, and the 13 pitfalls we encountered.

item.title: DBA Agent in Action: 10 Thousand Tickets and 99.6% Automation of the Second-Line Support
item.description:
Hello, Habr! This is the fourth article in a series about R&D research for a small DBA team. We started by deciding to simplify the monitoring of our fleet of over 800 instances of our Platform V Pangolin DB DBMS (a relational DBMS based on PostgreSQL) by modifying postgres_exporter. Then, we built an autonomous agent that handles tickets itself: it cleans disk space, performs VACUUM/ANALYZE, and schedules DB shutdowns. In this article, I'll explain how we continued to test the agent hypothesis: moved it to second-line support mode and measured the real results. There will be numbers, examples, the use of LLM for pattern analysis, migration of tasks from Pipeliner, and plans for further R&D and transforming the agent into a full-fledged second-line support.

item.title: RSI became the new AGI. Let's analyze why this is a misrepresentation
item.description:
In September 2026, the industry is once again debating what constitutes human-level artificial intelligence – artificial general intelligence (AGI). A convenient answer has emerged: AGI will be achieved when AI can conduct AI research and create its successor, i.e., upon achieving recursive self-improvement (RSI). 1. I'll start with definitions to avoid confusion. AGI (artificial general intelligence) describes the breadth of capabilities: a system is considered general when it can perform most economically valuable tasks at a human level. RSI (recursive self-improvement) describes the mechanism of development: a system improves itself or its successor, with each improvement facilitating the next. ASI (artificial superintelligence) describes the level of capabilities: a system surpasses all humans in virtually everything. These three axes: Read more

item.title: AGI as a Cognitive OS: What if We Look for Programs, Not Weights?
item.description:
Imagine you're handed a system for support. It works—and works brilliantly: writes code, translates, reasons, jokes. No documentation. No source code. Just a binary of several hundred gigabytes and a log of how it was compiled. When asked "how does it work inside?" the team honestly shrugs. This is roughly what large language models look like today. We've learned to compile intelligence from data, but we haven't learned to write—or even properly read—its source code. Read more

item.title: Why You Shouldn't Give 100% of Your Thinking to AI: The Trap of Blind Trust in AI Assistants
item.description:
We live in an era where AI is no longer a promised revolution but sits in a neighboring tab. ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, Copilot write code faster than us, generate tests, explain concepts, and help with architecture. Behind this convenience lies a silent professional trap. Many are starting to delegate not just routine tasks to models, but the very process of thinking. This doesn't look like degradation in the first month; it looks like productivity. It ends with a person unable to understand their own code without a chat. Below, without moralizing: where the red line is, what blind trust looks like in practice, and how to use AI so it remains an exoskeleton, not a prosthesis. Read more

item.title: AI Agents in Investments: Building a Telegram Assistant and Trading Bot with Tinkoff Investments MCP
item.description:
Hello, Habr! I'm Alexey Kabanov, a developer in the Tinkoff Investments public API team. We recently launched an MCP server that allows AI agents to interact with Tinkoff Investments: search for suitable securities, analyze the market, and a client's portfolio. I'll explain how to build automation based on AI agents using our MCP server. Not long ago, to automate even a simple trading algorithm, you had to write your own script: Python, broker API, cron, and error handling for all life's situations. Professional trading systems existed before, but the entry barrier for individual investors remained high. Now, there's a standard layer between LLMs and broker APIs — MCP, Model Context Protocol: the model can get the portfolio state, view the order book, place or cancel an order, and you just need to describe the task in human language. Tinkoff Investments has a public MCP server, and this article is about how to use it. The client can be anything: an AI agent like Hermes Agent, an automation platform like n8n, a desktop assistant, an IDE. We'll explore how these approaches differ and how they work with MCP, what the server can do, and then build two working examples. Read on
